preps.texto:
**Who she is.** Career coach at Bentley's CareerEdge, seven years there, ex-recruiter at a Boston consulting firm. Your first session was three weeks ago; she told you the US reads your directness as pressure.

**Last time.** You brought the Grupo Ferra story. She cut it to two sentences and asked you to say *what changed for them* before *what you built*.

**What she asked.** Bring the a16z Academy answers, draft or not, and one US cold message you actually sent.

**The one ask.** Ask her which three of your Academy answers she would cut in half, and why those three.

**Bring.** The Academy draft (three answers done, two open), the Nathan Okafor follow-up, the one-pager.

**Avoid.** Defending the long answers. She is the audience you are writing for.

**Who she is.** Bentley '24, Chief Business Officer at G19 Studio — a 14-person Boston studio that builds custom AI for mid-size firms (distributors, clinics, a law firm). She runs sales and scoping; the founder runs the engineers. Prof. Alan Purcell introduced you by mail five days ago; she answered in two lines the same day.

**Last time.** Never met. One thread: she said yes to 30 minutes and asked you to "bring campaigns or content you've made".

**What she asked for.** Content, not credentials. She wants to see how you explain AI to people who do not code — that is what G19 sells and what they lack in Spanish-speaking markets.

**The one ask.** Ask her what a G19 engagement looks like from first call to signed scope, and where the handoff to the client's own people breaks.

**Bring.** The Grupo Ferra one-pager (text only), the 1,200-view post on explaining AI without the hype, two of the training clips you recorded for the Ferra supervisors, and the workflow analogy.

**Avoid.** Pitching yourself for a job. She is a peer with a pipeline, not a recruiter; the win is one shared client or a referral in Monterrey.

**Who he is.** Partnerships lead at NEST, a Cambridge hardware incubator (twelve companies a cohort, two cohorts a year). MIT '19, mechanical engineering; three years at a robotics startup before NEST. He found you through the post on explaining AI without the hype and wrote first.

**Last time.** Never met. Two short mails: he wants "someone who can explain AI to our founders without the hype" — his founders build physical products and get sold AI every week.

**What he asked for.** A conversation, no deck. He said twice that his founders are tired of vendors.

**The one ask.** Ask him which of the twelve founders in the current cohort has a product where AI changes the margin, and whether NEST pays for a workshop or expects it as a favor.

**Bring.** Three questions for a founder, not a pitch; the Ferra supervisor story (training in the plant, no slides); your line: the AI adapts to the worker, not the worker to the AI.

**Avoid.** Offering a free workshop in the first ten minutes. Let him name the format.

preps.nota: 2 Areas/Agenda/Preps/Prep — MIT AI Club Founders night.md
preps.evento: MIT AI Club — Founders & Builders night
preps.texto:
**What it is.** The MIT AI Club's monthly open night: three founders talk for ten minutes each, then an hour of mingling. Open to non-MIT people with a sign-up; you registered in two days ago (confirmation in your MIT inbox).

**Who will be there.** The club's co-president Lena Hartwig (MIT '27) runs the speaker calendar. Two of the three speakers are hardware founders — one came through NEST, which is your bridge from the Matthew Hale meeting.

**Last time.** You have not been to one. Ernesto Salinas said he would come; he has been silent for nine days, so plan as if he will not.

**The one ask.** Ask them who decides the spring speaker list and whether a non-MIT consultant can give a 20-minute talk on explaining AI to a factory floor.

**Bring.** Twenty cards, the one-pager on your phone, three names you want to leave with. Say Monterrey early — it is the thing people remember.

**Avoid.** Staying with the Mexicans in the room. Two conversations with strangers before you find anyone you know.

preps.evento: Daniela Ruiz — Grupo Ferra, scope review
preps.texto:
**Who she is.** Operations director at Grupo Ferra (Monterrey, about 200 people, metal parts for appliance makers). Your client since July; she sponsors the AI program with the board. Her board decides on phase two in two days.

**Last time.** Ten days ago, the scope meeting: you proposed three work streams; she pushed back on the second (quality photos) because the plant floor lacks lighting. You agreed to start with the two others.

**What she asked.** Two questions by mail: who owns the data after phase two, and what happens if the supervisors stop using the tool. Exo drafted the reply; you have not sent it.

**The one ask.** Ask her what the board said no to, in their words, before you present anything.

**Bring.** The phase-two scope with the two streams, the usage numbers from phase one (31 of 38 supervisors active last week), the data-ownership clause in plain Spanish.

**Avoid.** Adding a third stream to compensate. Smaller and finished beats bigger and open.
